title: Signal Lock — choose its world
question: Each direction supports the same round rules, simulated audience, and three knobs. Choose the world you want to play in.

options.label: Pocket theatre
options.lineage: Puppet rehearsal stages and theatre cue sheets
options.thesis: The audience casts a character; your knobs bring its double onto the stage.
materials: ink stage and cream cue strip
options.viewport: A huge paired character stage above three tactile controls; a cue strip makes open, restricted and frozen phases visible.
options.risk: The stage must stay spacious without hiding votes or making controls theatrical props.

raised.raise: One phase change coordinates the whole stage; panels never animate independently.
Movement stays confined to changing state so the reading field remains quiet.
The message inspector opens in place and returns to the same round.
Labels keep fixed positions so changing votes remain easy to compare.
Every mascot reads as a distinct silhouette at phone size.

options.label: Character press
options.lineage: Screen-print workshops and interchangeable toy moulds
options.thesis: Three ingredients stamp a living mascot into a bold colour-block playfield.
options.viewport: A blue character assembly field fills the left, a huge timer and vote strips sit right, and cream knobs run across the bottom.
options.risk: Playful toy interfaces are familiar; the composition and transitions must carry the originality.

options.label: The desk instrument
options.thesis: A playable tabletop console where every vote and turn has a physical response.
options.viewport: A single instrument fills the screen: a full-colour target window, voting meters, and three oversized detented knobs.
options.risk: Hardware styling can become dense; the mascot must stay colourful and readable.
options.case: Stronger control clarity; the theatre carries the shared classroom performance more naturally.

options.label: Unfolding sheet
options.thesis: Votes unfold a linked character assembly.
options.viewport: Linked folded cells reveal target and controls.
options.risk: Crease geometry competes with quick animal recognition.
options.case: Weaker classroom identification and slower target reading.

options.label: Spectral edge
options.thesis: Votes change a narrow band around an otherwise quiet playfield.
options.viewport: Characters sit in a quiet white field with spectral state edges.
options.risk: Delicate colour is a poor carrier for projector-visible game urgency.
options.case: Less connected to collaborative play and weaker phase visibility.
options.kept: Keep motion local to state changes.

options.label: Painted card stack
options.thesis: Editable game cards expose the machinery of play.
options.viewport: A fixed card holds characters, controls and an editable message panel.
options.risk: A strictly monochrome world cannot show the game's four colours faithfully.
options.case: Colour is a core game fact; this system obscures it.
options.kept: Inspect in place without losing context.

options.label: Departure board
options.thesis: Targets arrive as synchronized rows of flipping choices.
options.viewport: Animal, colour and accessory update in aligned departure rows.
options.risk: Text-first cells weaken composite mascot recognition and crowd the controls.
options.case: Less immediate than characters for this audience and this matching task.

options.label: Four-shade handheld
options.thesis: The round becomes a miniature sprite-matching game.
options.viewport: A compact sprite field uses two buttons and a directional pad.
options.risk: Four greens hide the red, blue, green and yellow distinction; two buttons conflict with three knobs.
options.case: The strict palette and controls distort game facts.

canonCard.label: Classic game screen
canonCard.thesis: A familiar quiz-game layout with a target, timer, score and control panels.
canonCard.viewport: A centered target above three equal control panels and a simple scoreboard.
canonCard.risk: Clear and familiar, but less distinctive.
